prompt: Data modelling is usually the first step in database design. What diagram does it produce?

options.text: A Data Flow Diagram
An Entity-Relationship Diagram
A sequence diagram
A deployment diagram

explanation: Data modelling analyses data objects and their relationships and produces an ERD.

why.a: Wrong. The DFD comes from process modelling.
why.c: Wrong. Sequence diagrams show object interaction over time.
why.d: Wrong. Deployment diagrams show hardware and software placement.

prompt: Match each description with the diagram the course text attaches it to.

pairs.left: What does the system DO with data?
What data must the system KEEP, and how is it connected?

pairs.right: Shown by the DFD, the process view
Shown by the ERD, the data view

explanation: The DFD shows verbs, what is done; the ERD shows nouns, what is kept. Together they are the full requirements picture before a database is built.

prompt: True or false: the course text says the ERD shows the verbs of the system and the DFD shows the nouns.
explanation: The other way round: the DFD shows the verbs, what the system does; the ERD shows the nouns, what it keeps.

prompt: What does the course text mean by saying a data model is INDEPENDENT of database technology?

options.text: The same model could be implemented in Microsoft Access, MySQL or any other system without changing the design
The model can only be built without any computer
The model does not need entities
The model must be redrawn for each database product

explanation: The design stands apart from the product, so it moves between database systems unchanged.

why.a: Correct. That is the independence the text describes.
why.b: Wrong. Not what independence means here.
why.c: Wrong. Entities are one of the four core elements.
why.d: Wrong. Independence means it does NOT need redrawing.

prompt: Which two of these are benefits of data modelling in the course text?

options.text: It exposes business rules and constraints before they are buried in program code
It removes the need for a DFD
It provides a stable foundation for physical database design
It guarantees the project finishes early

explanation: Benefits: clarifies what data to store; stable foundation for physical design; better communication between analysts, designers and users; exposes business rules and constraints early.

why.a: Correct. Rules and constraints are exposed early.
why.b: Wrong. The DFD and ERD work together.
why.c: Correct. Tables, columns and keys derive from it.

prompt: Match each ERD element with how the course text draws or describes it.

pairs.right: A rectangle named with a singular noun
An oval connected to its entity
The attribute that uniquely identifies each instance, the primary key
A line named with an active verb, such as Registers

explanation: The four ERD elements: entities, attributes, identifiers and relationships. In the text's construction steps the relationship verb sits in a DIAMOND on the line.

prompt: Why does the course text say a single named person, such as one particular student, is NOT an entity?

options.text: Because an entity always has more than one instance; the category the person belongs to is the entity
Because people can never be entities
Because entities must be objects, not people
Because entities are named with verbs

explanation: An entity ALWAYS has more than one instance. Student is the entity; one particular student is an instance of it.

why.a: Correct. One instance is not an entity; the category is.
why.b: Wrong. A person is one of the kinds of thing an entity can be.
why.c: Wrong. Entities can be persons, places, objects, events or concepts.
why.d: Wrong. Entities take singular nouns; relationships take verbs.

prompt: True or false: an entity should be named with a singular noun, such as Student rather than Students.
explanation: Singular noun, drawn as a rectangle.

why.false: Wrong. The text gives exactly this rule and example.

prompt: True or false: the course text advises including every attribute you can think of, since extra attributes cost nothing.
explanation: Include only the attributes the organisation needs: every extra one adds a column to store, validate and maintain.

why.true: Wrong. The text warns that extra attributes have a cost.

prompt: An Address attribute is broken down into Street, City and State. What kind of attribute is Address?

options.text: An identifier
A composite attribute
An associative entity
A relationship

explanation: A composite attribute can be broken into smaller attributes, drawn as smaller ovals branching off it.

why.a: Wrong. An identifier uniquely identifies an instance.
why.c: Wrong. An associative entity resolves many-to-many.

prompt: Why do systems prefer an assigned ID number over a phone number or email address as an identifier?

options.text: A good identifier should never be blank and never need to change once assigned
ID numbers are shorter to type
Phone numbers are not attributes
Emails cannot be stored in a database

explanation: Phone numbers and emails can be missing or change; an assigned ID never does.

why.c: Wrong. They are attributes, just poor identifiers.
why.d: Wrong. They can be stored; they just make poor keys.

prompt: Match each property of a relationship line with its meaning.

pairs.right: How many instances of one entity relate to the other
Whether the relationship is mandatory or optional

explanation: Three properties form the relationship statement: what (the verb), how many (cardinality), and must or may (ordinality).

prompt: Match each cardinality with the course text's example.

pairs.right: Each employee has one login account, each account belongs to one employee
One customer places many orders, each order belongs to one customer
A student registers for many courses, a course has many students

explanation: Three cardinalities. Many-to-many is resolved with an associative entity, such as Enrolment, when tables are built.

prompt: How is a many-to-many relationship normally resolved when an ERD is converted into database tables?

options.text: By deleting one of the entities
By introducing an associative entity, such as Enrolment or Registration
By making it one-to-one
By adding a composite attribute

explanation: An associative entity sits between the two, turning one M:N into two 1:M relationships.

why.a: Wrong. Both entities are still needed.
why.c: Wrong. That would change the business rule.
why.d: Wrong. Composite attributes break an attribute into parts.

prompt: A Course may exist in the catalogue before any student registers. What does that say about the Course side of the relationship?

options.text: Its ordinality is optional, a minimum of zero
Its ordinality is mandatory, a minimum of one
Its cardinality is one-to-one
It is a composite attribute

explanation: Ordinality is the MINIMUM: zero is optional, one is mandatory. A course with no students yet is optional; a student required to have an enrolment is mandatory.

why.b: Wrong. Mandatory would require at least one student.
why.c: Wrong. Cardinality counts the maximum, and a course has many students.

prompt: True or false: ordinality states whether the MINIMUM number of instances required is zero (optional) or one (mandatory).
explanation: Ordinality is the minimum; cardinality is how many.

why.false: Wrong. The text defines ordinality this way.

prompt: True or false: an ERD is read one relationship line at a time, in both directions.
explanation: One Course Section has many Enrolments, each for one Student; and one Student has many Enrolments, each for one Course Section.

why.true: Correct. One line at a time, both ways.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: What is the correct order of the five steps to construct an ER diagram?

options.text: Entities; attributes and identifier; relationship verb; cardinality; draw
Draw; entities; cardinality; attributes; relationship
Actors; use cases; diagram; narrative; review
Cardinality; entities; draw; attributes; relationship

explanation: Identify entities; identify attributes and mark the identifier; name the relationship with a verb; determine cardinality; draw, with rectangles, a labelled diamond, cardinality on either side, and attribute ovals.

why.a: Correct. The five steps in order.
why.b: Wrong. Drawing is the last step.
why.c: Wrong. Those are use-case modelling steps.
why.d: Wrong. Cardinality needs the entities and relationship first.

prompt: True or false: in the course text's drawing step, entities are connected through a relationship DIAMOND labelled with the verb.
explanation: Rectangles for entities, a diamond with the verb, cardinality on either side, ovals for attributes: Chen notation.

why.true: Correct. The diamond carries the verb.
why.false: Wrong. The text draws the relationship as a diamond.

prompt: In the course text's worked university ERD, what is the cardinality of 'Student Registers for Course', and why?

options.text: One-to-one, because each student takes one course
One-to-many, because one course has many students
Many-to-many, because one student registers for many courses and one course has many students
Zero-to-one, because registration is optional

explanation: Both directions are many: student_id identifies Student, course_code identifies Course, and the relationship is many-to-many.

why.a: Wrong. A student registers for many courses.
why.b: Wrong. It is many in BOTH directions, not just one.
why.d: Wrong. That is ordinality, not the cardinality asked for.

prompt: True or false: a relationship is usually named with an active verb, so the diagram reads like a sentence: Student Registers for Course.
explanation: Active verbs such as Registers, Teaches or Supervises make the ERD read as sentences.

why.false: Wrong. The text gives this rule and example.

prompt: An ERD is built from four main elements. Which two of these are among them?

options.text: Identifiers
Data stores
Attributes
Lifelines

explanation: Entities, attributes, identifiers and relationships.

why.b: Wrong. Data stores are DFD elements.
why.d: Wrong. Lifelines belong to sequence diagrams.
